---
title: The Galaxy Population & Weak-Lensing Framework
---

NumCosmo builds a galaxy weak-lensing likelihood out of small, single-purpose
pieces rather than one monolithic class per survey. This page is the map: the
vocabulary shared by every piece, how they nest into a pipeline, and how a
single galaxy's data flows through it. It does not derive any physics ---
the shape forward model lives on the
[Weak-Lensing Ellipticity](wl_ellipticity.qmd) page, the projected mass on
[Weak-Lensing Surface Mass Density](../wl/wl_surface_mass_density.qmd) --- this page
is about the *shape* of the code, so that those physics pages (and the
classes themselves) are easier to place. To see the framework used end to
end, generating a mock catalog, see the
[Simulating a Weak-Lensing Galaxy Catalog](../../../../tutorials/python/galaxy_wl_mock.qmd)
tutorial.

## Three Kinds of Object

Every galaxy observable (sky position, redshift, shape) is described by up to
three collaborating objects, distinguished by what they own and where they
live:

Models ([[math|NcmModel]] subclasses, registered in an [[math|NcmMSet]])
carry the *fitted parameters* of a pure conditional density. They are
evaluated at values handed to them; they never integrate, never touch a
catalog row, never know how many galaxies exist. A model is where a sampler
or optimizer looks for degrees of freedom.

Calculators (plain `GObject`s, *not* models, *not* in the `MSet`) own the
*mechanism*: the per-galaxy data layout, the file/catalog I/O, the generative
draw, and --- where relevant --- the marginalization/integration recipe. A
calculator reads whichever models it needs from an [[numcosmo-math|NcmMSet]] passed into each
call; it never stores a reference to one --- mirroring the
[[numcosmo|NcDistance]] pattern of resolving cosmology on every call rather
than caching it.

Orchestrators sit above the calculators and wire a fixed pipeline of
them together for a specific likelihood or generator (e.g.
[[numcosmo|NcDataClusterWLFactor]]); see [Current Status](#sec-status).

Distinguishing calc-vs-model is mostly by *type*, reinforced by naming: a
bare object name ([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftFactor]]) is a calculator; a name with a
role suffix ([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftPop]], [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopGauss]]) is a model.

## The Role Vocabulary

Within each physical quantity (redshift, position, shape), models and
calculators are named by the *role* they play, not by which survey or
implementation they encode. The reserved role tokens are:

- `Pop` --- the distribution of a galaxy population's *true* property,
  $p(\mathrm{true})$, e.g. $p(z)$ for the redshift distribution of a source
  sample ([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftPop]],
  [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftPopLSSTSRD]]) or $p(\chi_I)$ for the intrinsic
  ellipticity of a population ([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopGauss]],
  [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopBeta]]).
- `Obs` --- the observational model for a *single* object,
  $p(d \mid \mathrm{true})$, whose scatter is per-galaxy *data* (e.g. each
  galaxy's own photo-$z$ error $\sigma_0$,
  [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftObsGauss]]).
- `ObsSel` --- the *population-level* observable law, also
  $p(d \mid \mathrm{true})$ but as a mixture over per-object scatter whose
  width is a fitted population parameter, not per-galaxy data. Its windows
  define observable-space selection and marginals such as $P(z_p)$. `Obs` and
  `ObsSel` are different mathematical objects (single-object conditional vs.
  population mixture) that only happen to coincide for a Gaussian kernel.
- `Factor` --- the likelihood-factor *calculator role*: a normalized
  conditional density that (a) composes multiplicatively / by marginalization
  into a data likelihood, and (b) doubles as a generative node for sampling
  (every `Factor` draws an observation: `gen`, or for the shape factor `gen_shear`,
  which draws at a given reduced shear). [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftFactor]] assembles the
  per-observation redshift factor $p(z_p, z)$; [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapeFactor]] the
  per-observation shape factor $p(\epsilon_\mathrm{obs} \mid g)$ at the reduced shear $g$.
  Note the factors are a *mix* of priors (`Pop` terms) and likelihoods (`Obs`
  terms) --- "factor in the computation of the (marginal) likelihood," not
  "every factor is itself a likelihood."
- `Binning` --- a distinct calculator role, standalone rather than a
  `Factor` scheme: the dn/dz and $P(z_p)$ population-level query
  ([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftBinning]]), consumed by cross-correlation
  tooling independently of any per-galaxy likelihood.

Where a calculator role has more than one implementation strategy, they are
*schemes* sharing one abstract base --- e.g. [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftFactorComposed]]
(true-$z$ kernel $\otimes$ photo-$z$ error kernel) is one scheme of
[[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftFactor]], mirroring how [[numcosmo|NcPowspecMLTransfer]] and
friends are schemes of [[math|NcmPowspec]]. The scheme name is appended
after the role (`Factor` + `Composed`), never a numerical-method name.

## The Fixed Pipeline: Z $\Rightarrow$ P $\Rightarrow$ S {#sec-fixed-pipeline}

A galaxy observation combines three factors in a fixed order (redshift, then
position, then shape) because each later stage conditions on the earlier ones: the
reduced shear at the galaxy depends on its source redshift and its position, and the
position can, in general, depend on the redshift. What is pluggable is *within* each
level (which scheme, which models fill its slots), never the
Z $\Rightarrow$ P $\Rightarrow$ S order itself.

The per-galaxy fragments of the three factors are siblings: each is created by its own
factor and reads and writes its own catalog columns. [[numcosmo|NcDataClusterWLFactor]]
keeps, for each galaxy, a record of four parts: the position fragment
([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyPositionFactorData]]), the redshift fragment
([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftFactorData]]), the halo weak-lensing fragment
([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyHaloWLData]]) and the shape fragment
([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapeFactorData]]). Each object receives only its part: the position
factor the position, [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyHaloWL]] the position and its own fragment,
[[numcosmo|NcWLClusterLens]] the surface densities of that fragment and the source redshift, and
the shape factor its own fragment and the reduced shear $g$, in the frame of the
galaxy's ellipticity, at which it evaluates the marginal.
[[numcosmo|nc_data_cluster_wl_factor_required_columns]] lists the catalog columns of the
whole record.

The quantities of a galaxy that depend on its position relative to the halo belong to
[[numcosmo|NcGalaxyHaloWL]]. It is not a factor, but it has a per-galaxy fragment,
[[numcosmo|NcGalaxyHaloWLData]], with the projected radius $R$, the rotation factor
$e^{2i\phi}$ of the azimuth $\phi$ of the galaxy around the halo center, and the surface
densities $\Sigma(R)$ and $\bar\Sigma(<R)$. [[numcosmo|NcWLClusterLens]] computes the
tangential reduced shear $g_t(z)$ from the surface densities and the critical surface
density at the source redshift $z$. [[numcosmo|NcDataClusterWLFactor]] forms the shear
$g = (1 + m)\, g_t(z)\, e^{2i\phi} + c$ of each galaxy in the frame of its
ellipticity and passes it to the shape factor.

A stage that needs a quantity of another part, for example a clustered position scheme
reading the source redshift for magnification bias, receives that part from the data
object; the parts stay separate.

## Data Objects: Fragments, Vtables, and the Catalog

Every calculator's per-galaxy `...Data` struct ([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyRedshiftFactorData]],
[[numcosmo|NcGalaxyPositionFactorData]], [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapeFactorData]], and each `Pop`
model's `...PopData`) follows the same small idiom, so that any of them can be
stored, generated, or replayed the same way:

- a few typed public fields for the universal, always-present part of the
  observation (e.g. `z`, `ra`/`dec`, `epsilon_obs_1/2`);
- an opaque `ldata` pointer for whatever the concrete scheme/model needs
  that isn't universal (e.g. the Composed redshift scheme's cached
  $\{z_p, \sigma_0\}$ fragment, or a `Pop` model's resolved
  $\{\sigma, \mathrm{norm}\}$);
- a fragment vtable of four function pointers travelling with `ldata`:
  `ldata_read_row`, `ldata_write_row`, `ldata_required_columns`, and
  `ldata_destroy`. These are set once, in the constructing scheme's
  `data_init`, and never switched on again afterwards --- so reading/writing a
  row is a plain vtable call, not a per-row type dispatch.

`ldata_required_columns` takes a `GList **` (not `GList *`): each level
*appends* its own column names to the list threaded down from its caller, so
the columns needed by a whole pipeline (position + redshift + shape) can be
collected by concatenating what every level reports, with no level needing to
know the others' column names in advance.

The catalog these rows are read from and written to is
[[numcosmo|NcGalaxyWLObs]] --- a plain matrix of named `double` columns (an
[[math|NcmCatalog]] subclass) with one extra per-row field for a photo-$z$
spline, plus the ellipticity convention ($\chi$ vs. $\epsilon$) and
handedness frame it was recorded in. It carries *no* calculator- or
model-specific knowledge: it is just storage, addressed by column name. A
factor's `data_new(calculator, mset, ...)` allocates the typed fragments (a
model-identity-dependent, param-*independent* layout, so it is safe to reuse
across every galaxy and every `prepare()` in an MCMC chain --- no per-step
reallocation); `write_row`/`read_row` move a fragment to/from one row of the
shared [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyWLObs]].

## Caches and the Hot-Loop Discipline

A galaxy's shape likelihood is evaluated at many source-redshift nodes during
one $z$-integral, and that integral runs once per galaxy per likelihood
evaluation --- so anything that does *not* depend on the integration variable
must be computed exactly once per galaxy, not once per node. This discipline
shows up as two kinds of cache:

Per-galaxy halo quantities ([[numcosmo|NcGalaxyHaloWLData]]): $R$, $e^{2i\phi}$,
$\Sigma(R)$ and $\bar\Sigma(<R)$ do not depend on the source redshift.
[[numcosmo|NcDataClusterWLFactor]] recomputes $R$ and $e^{2i\phi}$ when the radius hash
of [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyHaloWL]] changes (the halo position and the cosmology), and the
surface densities when the profile hash of [[numcosmo|NcWLClusterLens]] changes (the
cosmology, the density profile, its mass summary and the halo position). Under the
`CHEB_WEIGHTS` method the critical surface density at the redshift nodes of each galaxy
is computed once and recomputed when the geometry hash of the lens changes (the
cosmology and the cluster redshift). At a node only the reduced shear is formed from
these values, and the shape factor receives it in the frame of the galaxy's
ellipticity, so no marginalization subclass repeats this work per node.

Per-galaxy resolved model state (`ldata` on a `Pop` model's `...Data`):
the same principle applies one level down. [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopGaussLocal]], for
instance, must invert a per-galaxy target $e_\mathrm{rms}$ into the internal
Gaussian width $\sigma$ by bisection --- an $O(\log)$ root-find that would be
wasteful to repeat at every $z$-node, so the calculators keep to a strict rule: anything that
does not depend on the integration variable is resolved once, in `prepare()`,
never inside the marginalization loop. [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopGaussLocal]]'s
`prepare()` vfunc runs the bisection once per galaxy and caches
$\{\sigma, \sigma^{-2}/2, \mathrm{norm}\}$ into `ldata`; `eval_p`,
called once per node thereafter, only ever reads the cache.

### Optional Capabilities via the Data Vtable

The same per-galaxy `...Data` struct is also how a model advertises an
*optional* capability to a consumer it doesn't otherwise know about, without
resorting to a concrete-type check. [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopData]] carries a fifth,
optional vtable slot,

```c
gdouble (*ldata_get_sigma) (NcGalaxyShapePopData *data);
```

`NULL` unless the concrete `Pop` model parameterizes its density through an
(untruncated) Gaussian width --- true for both [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopGauss]]
(Global) and [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopGaussLocal]] (per-galaxy), false for
[[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopBeta]]. [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapeFactorVarAdd]] (the variance-add
marginalization scheme) needs exactly this width and gets it through the
base-level dispatcher `nc_galaxy_shape_pop_get_sigma()`, which reads the slot
and raises a clear error if it is `NULL`. This is the reason
[[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopGaussLocal]] is a *parallel type* to [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePopGauss]] --- both
derive directly from [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyShapePop]] and fill this slot with the same
function --- rather than a subclass kept around only so a concrete type-check
would accept it: the capability the consumer needs is expressed on the shared
data, not on the class hierarchy.

## Generation and Likelihood Use the Same Shear {#sec-gen-like}

The shape factor draws an observed ellipticity with `gen_shear` and evaluates the
likelihood factor with `eval_shear`. Both take the reduced shear of the galaxy and the
same per-galaxy data; there is no separate simulation-mode struct.
[[numcosmo|NcDataClusterWLFactor]] forms that shear in the same way for `resample` and
for the likelihood, so the mock catalog and the likelihood use the same frame, sign and
calibration order. The
[Simulating a Weak-Lensing Galaxy Catalog](../../../../tutorials/python/galaxy_wl_mock.qmd)
tutorial forms the shear by hand from [[numcosmo|NcGalaxyHaloWL]] and
[[numcosmo|NcWLClusterLens]], draws a catalog with `gen_shear`, and evaluates the
likelihood factor of a galaxy of that catalog with `eval_shear`.

## Current Status {#sec-status}

As of this writing, the redshift (`Composed`, `Spline` schemes), position
(`Flat` scheme), and shape (`VarAdd`, `MomentsGauss`, `MomentsTilt`, `Spectral`
marginalization schemes) factors are implemented, and
[[numcosmo|NcDataClusterWLFactor]] wires them into a single orchestrator
that resolves models from an [[numcosmo-math|NcmMSet]] and runs the per-galaxy
$z$-integral automatically.
